It had been five years since the event, since the mass exodus from the cities, the frantic scramble for resources, the utter collapse of civilization and the subsequent rise of the hordes. Five years of walking this blasted land, scavenging what little survived, and generally avoiding trouble. It had been five years since I'd last encountered a human.

The first thing Lieutenant Commander Alistair Campbell saw was blood. A thick, sticky crimson coating the metallic floor of the corridor, spattered on the walls. That was the first thing. The second was the silence. No screams, no battle cries, no alarm bells.

Just blood and silence.

Alistair pushed himself up. He was still wearing his standard issue X4 battle armor, the reinforced plating groaning slightly as he shifted his weight. He took a breath and activated the helmet’s diagnostics. “Systems nominal,” a monotone synthesized voice crackled in his ear. He pulled out his laser pistol and activated the light.

The scene below illuminated – at least, to the limited range of his helmet’s illumination. He still wasn’t quite seeing what the hell had just happened. The entire corridor was a mess. Twisted metal, fractured concrete, a carpet of gore. Soldiers lay scattered, their armor torn open, limbs missing. And next to them, a group of Z’tharr.

The Z’tharr, if you hadn’t met one in your brief service in the Orion Arm, were, to put it mildly, unsettling creatures. They were insectoid in nature, their bodies covered in thick, chitinous armor plates. They stood about 6 feet tall with a slender, almost emaciated frame, moving with a jerky, unsettling gait. Their heads were small, smooth domes with large, black, multifaceted eyes. They had no mouths. They fed through their skin, absorbing nutrients from the environment. And, according to the battle briefing, they were exceptionally nasty.

They were also now dead.

Or at least, most of them were. Scattered around the room were six of the creatures, their bodies partially melted into the ground. It looked like acid had been splashed over them. Campbell ran a quick scan of the area. The X4's long-range sensors detected no immediate threats. The air was clean, with a slight metallic tang, and he could detect a lingering, acrid smell.

I was a cartographer. Not the grand, majestic type. I was the sort of person you'd stumble upon in a dusty corner of a sprawling town, maybe after a long, winding road. I lived in a little cottage on the edge of the Silverwood Forest, and I made maps for those who needed them. I charged three copper pieces a scroll, plus one silver for detailing. Not much, but enough to keep me going.

My name is Silas. Or at least, that’s what I was called.

I hadn’t been called anything else until this whole mess started.

Before, people called me Silas. They'd ask for maps of the Black Mountains, or the Dragon's Tooth Pass, or even just to show their friends, “Look, Silas made this!” And then they'd go on their way, leaving me to my parchment and my pens.

That was the time before.

It's strange how quickly things can change.

"You must have been waiting for me?" I scoffed, a guttural rumble in my chest. The air around the little shack seemed to crackle with barely contained fury. I burst out laughing, but it was a mirthless sound. "Rehabilitate? Observe? For the last decade, you have confined me to this... this hovel and made me watch the same exercises over and over again!
